Financial markets are one of the greatest inventions of human thought, and one of its greatest expressions of judgment. Every price is a compressed argument: millions of people reading the same numbers, the same filings, the same news, and placing their judgment against one another's. What comes out is our best collective guess about the future, revised every second.

For as long as financial markets have existed, only people could take part in that argument. Machines could count, store and execute, often faster than any of us, yet they could not read a company's story and form a view of it. The building blocks of the financial markets, a balance sheet, a quarter's results, a chief executive choosing her words on a call, a line buried deep in a filing, were written for people, and only people could understand them.

This is no longer true. AI is beginning to understand what financial markets are made of. It can read the filing, follow the call, weigh the news against the numbers and say what it thinks it all means. And now something more is appearing: early signs of investment judgment. Not a summary of what happened, but a view of what happens next.

I don't think we've seen anything like this before. It is the new frontier of AI in the financial markets, and it's where Forward Model works.

## From signals to judgment.

Until now, the most advanced machines in finance were quantitative models. They searched prices and data for patterns, extracted signals, and traded them at a scale no person could match. The quant era changed the financial markets, and it gave finance something lasting: the discipline to measure, and the habit of trusting evidence over stories.

What is arriving now builds on that, and it is different in kind. These new models read. They take in a company's results, its filings, its calls and the news around it, and they weigh all of it together, the way a good analyst does, to form a view and explain it in plain words. For the first time, machines are beginning to form investment judgment of the kind that until now only people could.

We carry the quant era's discipline forward. What we measure with it is something new.

## The future is the only honest exam.

Every new kind of intelligence invites big claims. Most are tested on questions whose answers are already known, and anything that has seen the answers can look brilliant.

The financial markets don't work that way. No one has the answer key to next month. A view about the future is either borne out by what happens or it isn't, and there's no talking your way around it. This makes the financial markets the hardest and most honest test of judgment we have, for people and for machines alike.

So I believe machine judgment should be tested where it can't hide: committed before the outcome, graded by what happens next, and shown in full, including the days it's wrong.

## A portfolio is an expression of judgment. It isn't the purest one.

The obvious way to test a model is the way we have always tested people: give it money and watch the returns. Returns carry everything else along with the judgment: how much risk was taken, how each bet was sized, when it traded, what it paid to trade, and above all which way the market happened to go. Over weeks or months, returns are mostly luck, and even a genuinely skilled manager needs years before the record can tell skill from chance.

With AI we can do something we could never do with people. We can put a model in the most distilled setup there is, which I call a call harness. It's given everything it needs to make a call on a company, and it makes that call: a score, with the reasoning behind it, in plain words. Nothing sits between its judgment and the grade. It can make that call on every stock, every trading day, about 2,800 of them, and each one is checked against what happened next. Thousands of graded calls a day reveal in months what a portfolio can take years to show. We don't judge a weather forecaster by whether they got rich betting on the weather. We score every forecast. Machine judgment deserves the same.

## So we built our own.

The general frontier models are remarkable readers. Still, we felt there could be a new frontier out there: a model made for the financial markets that could read the same evidence better than they do, when the question is where a stock goes next. So we embarked on a long journey to search for it, and Forward Model MK1 is what we found: our own LLM, trained for the financial markets.

## Tested on days no model had seen.

We put Forward Model MK1 up against the leading frontier models: OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra, Google's Gemini 4 Argon, and Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1. Each day, every model was given the same stocks, the same context and the same prompt, through the same call harness. The test ran on seven trading days in September, all after every model's stated knowledge cutoff, so no model could have seen how those days turned out. It was a test of judgment, not memory. The market graded every score 21 trading days later, after taking out what the market, each stock's sector and its style explain. We wrote the rules before we read a single rival's answer.

It picked stocks better than the frontier models over the test week, and better than three of the four on every one of the seven days. Against Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1, the lead clears the bar we set before the test began. One week is one window, so the direction is clear. We've published the whitepaper.

## Why I started Forward Model

I started Forward Model as a research lab, to push the frontier of AI in the financial markets and deepen our understanding of investment judgment itself: what it is, where it comes from, and how far machines can take it. Financial markets ask the hardest questions any mind can face. How does a model read ambiguity, when the same sentence on a call can be a warning or a reassurance? How does it judge what a price already believes, and where that belief might be wrong? How do you train an LLM to exercise judgment, when the answer arrives a month after the question? How do you evaluate any LLM, from any lab, on judgment rather than memory? These are the questions we work on. We ship what we learn as products people can use every day, so the research is tested where it matters most.

We spent much of this year in stealth on exactly that work. We've made hundreds of thousands of scores, and we grade each one against what the market does over the next 21 trading days. The stocks scored higher have done better than the ones scored lower on almost every day we've graded, even after taking out what the market and common factors explain. We publish that record in full: every score sealed when it's published and graded in public afterwards, including any days below zero. We call that grade Forward Skill. It's what we answer to, and every new version of our model earns its own record. It's early, and the record is young, but we'd rather be measured than believed.

## Open to everyone.

If we stay relentlessly focused on raising Forward Skill, I have full conviction Forward Model MK1 becomes the intelligence you'll want across your entire investment workflow: scoring stocks every day, going deep on a single company, and thinking a hard decision through with you. Every one of those tasks rests on judgment. If you could work with a model that gets the financial markets right more often, and whose judgment has held up in public, day after day, I can't think of a reason you'd choose any other.

And I believe it should be open to everyone. The same judgment, on the same stocks, at the same time, whether you are an individual investor or you run one of the world's largest funds, with the same record behind it, in the open, where anyone can check it. We don't manage any investment capital, nor do we have any plans to. Instead, you can bring Forward Model MK1's scores and reasoning into Claude with our MCP connector, into your own code through our API, or talk with it directly in our chat, all in one plan.

I've never been more convinced of our mission: to research and develop the best intelligence for the financial markets, and to make it accessible to everyone. This is the frontier we intend to keep pushing.

Ehsan Yousefzadeh Founder & CEO, Forward Model
